title: The lift (Story of a Soul)
hook: Thérèse, too small to climb the stairs of perfection, looks for a lift: Jesus' arms
tomorrow: what do you do when you want every calling at once?

segments.voice: Last week ended on one leaf: love every leaf. This week's voices are small on purpose, and the first is a young nun who couldn't climb.
screen: `LOVE EVERY LEAF.` → `A WEEK OF SMALL VOICES.`

segments.voice: The feed is full of climbs: the internship, the personal best, the acceptance letter, each one another step up. A young nun in a French convent is writing down how that feels. Next to the saints, Thérèse says, she's a grain of sand beside a mountain whose peak is lost in the clouds. The stairs of perfection are long and rough, and she's too small to climb them. Anyone else might put the pen down there. She goes looking for another way up.
screen: `A FEED FULL OF CLIMBS.` → `A GRAIN OF SAND BY A MOUNTAIN.` → `TOO SMALL FOR THE STAIRS.`

segments.voice: She finds it in something new in her own day. In the houses of the rich, she writes, there are now lifts, elevators that carry you up without the stairs. She wants one: a lift to raise her to Jesus, since she's too little to climb the rough stairway of perfection. So she searches scripture, and finds two lines. The first, from Proverbs, is wisdom calling out: whoever is a little one, let him come to me. That's how her Latin Bible reads it. Here's the detail to tell a friend: the King James reads the same verse differently, “Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither.” The second is from Isaiah, where God speaks like a mother: “As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you.” Isaiah says the little ones will be carried, and rocked on the knees. That's her answer. The lift is the arms of Jesus. She doesn't need to grow strong enough to climb. She needs to stay little, even to become littler, and let herself be carried. It's an odd ambition. She still wants to be a saint; she says so. But her way runs through smallness, and up only because someone else lifts. She calls it a little way, and it's honest about what she can't do. No pretending the stairs are short. Just another way up.
screen: `LIFTS IN THE HOUSES OF THE RICH.` · `WHOEVER IS A LITTLE ONE.` · `CARRIED, AND ROCKED ON THE KNEES.` · `A LITTLE WAY UP.` · then, large: `HIS ARMS ARE THE LIFT.`

segments.voice: Let whatever is under you take your full weight: the chair, the floor, the bed. Loosen your shoulders, your jaw, your hands, and stop holding yourself up. Isaiah's picture can rest with you there: carried, comforted the way a mother comforts a child.
The lift. Thérèse's picture: too small for the stairs, she's carried up in the arms of Jesus.
The line to keep: his arms are the lift. She didn't get strong; she got carried. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1674 COUNTS.` → `SAINTS AND TEACHERS IN THEIR OWN WORDS · 73 OF 80.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT IF YOU WANT EVERY CALLING AT ONCE?`

howItsDone: Catholics honor Thérèse of Lisieux as a saint, and Christians of other churches read Story of a Soul too; her little way is taught as trusting God like a small child.

fork.setup: a friend says she's "not good enough to pray" after a rough year, so she's quitting until she's better. what fits Thérèse's lift?
options: get better first; come back once you can climb on your own.
you don't have to be strong enough. stay little, and let yourself be carried.
if you're not good enough, holiness probably isn't for you.
fork.reveal: Thérèse was too small for the stairs and didn't pretend otherwise. she asked to be carried, and called that her little way.

chat.says: can't hit the high note. director says stop pushing, let the choir hold you. i'm too small for this.
options: Then don't climb it alone. Like Thérèse's lift, let the choir carry you up to it.
Push harder in practice. Saints climb the stairs; you'll get there with effort.
Give the solo back. If you're too small, it isn't meant for you.
chat.meaning: Thérèse was too small for the stairs, so she let Jesus' arms be her lift. Being carried isn't failing; it's another way up.
